planets.name: HD 189733 b
planets.hook: A blue planet with a very different atmosphere
planets.intro: HD 189733 b is blue in reflected visible light. It circles its star in just over two days, surrounded by a hot atmosphere where telescopes have detected water vapour, carbon monoxide and hydrogen sulfide.
planets.question: How did we find out that it is blue?
planets.answer: Hubble measured how much visible light disappeared when the planet passed behind its star. More of the missing light was blue than red. The difference reveals the colour of the reflected light.
planets.evidence: The striking thing about HD 189733 b is that its blue colour comes from a measurement. In 2013, Thomas Evans and colleagues used Hubble to watch the planet disappear behind its star. The system lost more light in the blue part of the spectrum than at longer visible wavelengths. By measuring the missing light, they worked out the colour of the planet’s reflected light. Their results fit reflective clouds, with sodium absorbing some of the longer-wavelength light. That famous description brings together two ideas: mineral particles in the atmosphere and powerful winds. Silicate particles—made from the same broad family of materials used to make glass—could help scatter the light. If such particles form and settle, winds could carry them along. But the blue-colour measurement did not identify falling glass, and no one has observed a sideways glass shower. The evidence for moving air comes from a different experiment. Tom Louden and Peter Wheatley studied sodium absorption as the planet crossed its star. The absorption shifted in wavelength on opposite edges of the planet, revealing gas moving towards and away from us. Their 2015 analysis was consistent with planetary rotation and a strong eastward jet. It measured atmospheric motion, rather than the speed or direction of falling particles. In 2024, Guangwei Fu and colleagues used Webb to identify water vapour, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and hydrogen sulfide in light passing through the atmosphere. These gases absorb different infrared wavelengths, leaving patterns in the spectrum. Together, their inferred abundances point to an atmosphere enriched in heavier elements relative to its star—a clue to the material the planet gathered as it formed.

planets.name: HD 209458 b
planets.hook: An atmosphere revealed by a trace of sodium
planets.intro: HD 209458 b is a hot gas giant with sodium in its atmosphere. The sodium absorbs a small part of the starlight passing through the gas. This was the first exoplanet whose atmosphere was detected and chemically identified.
planets.question: How can a trace of sodium reveal a whole atmosphere?
planets.answer: Atoms absorb particular colours of light. When the planet crossed its star, the dip in brightness was slightly deeper at sodium’s wavelengths. Comparing neighbouring wavelengths isolated the extra absorption.
planets.evidence: During a transit, a little starlight passes through the rim of this planet’s atmosphere. Charbonneau and colleagues found an extra dip at the colours absorbed by sodium. That small difference, reported in 2002, became the first chemical identification of an exoplanet atmosphere. Later observations also detected water vapour.

planets.name: WASP-39 b
planets.hook: A giant with the mass of Saturn
planets.intro: WASP-39 b has roughly the mass of Saturn, spread across a globe larger than Jupiter. Its hot, hydrogen-rich atmosphere contains water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Beneath the clouds, the gas grows denser with depth, with no solid ground to stand on.
planets.question: What does the carbon dioxide do?
planets.answer: Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light, so it changes how heat moves through the atmosphere and escapes to space. Water vapour and other gases do this too. The amount of carbon dioxide matters, but it cannot tell us the whole climate on its own. This planet has a deep hydrogen-rich envelope.
planets.evidence: Webb caught starlight filtering through WASP-39 b and found a strong carbon-dioxide fingerprint. A second, initially puzzling feature pointed to sulfur dioxide. Photochemical models explained how stellar ultraviolet light could start reactions that make it. The spectrum therefore tells us both what is in the air and something about the chemistry happening there.

planets.name: WASP-107 b
planets.hook: Clouds made from rock minerals
planets.intro: WASP-107 b has an enormous atmosphere for its modest mass. Almost as wide as Jupiter, it has only about a tenth of Jupiter’s mass. Its clouds contain tiny silicate particles, made from the same family of minerals that forms much of Earth’s rock. Here, that material hangs high in a hot atmosphere.
planets.question: What keeps the cloud material aloft?
planets.answer: Atmospheric mixing can carry vapour and tiny particles upward. Cloud models reproduce the silicate feature when that mixing is included. The same atmosphere contains much less methane than simple equilibrium chemistry predicts.
planets.evidence: The broad infrared feature measured by Webb’s MIRI instrument fits tiny silicate grains suspended in the atmosphere. A later NIRSpec spectrum also detected methane, but far less than expected in gas at the upper atmosphere’s temperature. Models connect that shortage to mixing from a hotter interior. Combining the gases with the planet’s mass and size gives clues to what keeps this enormous atmosphere inflated.

planets.name: WASP-43 b
planets.hook: Clouds on the night side
planets.intro: WASP-43 b completes an orbit in about 20 hours and is expected to keep the same side facing its star. Its day-side atmosphere reaches roughly 1,250 °C, while even the night side is around 590 °C. Thick clouds probably cover the darker hemisphere, hiding the hotter gas below.
planets.question: How do we study the night side?
planets.answer: As the planet travels around its star, different parts of its globe face us. Following the changing infrared brightness lets astronomers compare the day and night hemispheres.
planets.evidence: Astronomers watched WASP-43 b throughout an orbit with Webb. As its bright and dark hemispheres turned into view, the changing infrared light revealed a hot day side and a much fainter night side. Models with clouds on the night side fit the observations: those clouds hide warmer gas underneath. The infrared observations measure the atmosphere’s heat, rather than a solid surface.

planets.name: WASP-121 b
planets.hook: Rock ingredients in gas form
planets.intro: The day side of WASP-121 b is so hot that some ingredients of rock remain in gas form. Its atmosphere contains silicon monoxide, a gas made of silicon and oxygen. The cooler night side contains methane, giving this giant different mixtures of gases on opposite sides.
planets.question: Can an atmosphere stretch around an orbit?
planets.answer: Helium observations detect absorption over a large fraction of the orbit. They support an extended outflow from the planet, far beyond the part of the atmosphere seen during an ordinary transit.
planets.evidence: Webb can compare the light arriving from this planet’s day and night hemispheres. The spectra reveal silicon monoxide and a striking chemical contrast, including methane on the cooler night side. At these temperatures, material that would form rock on Earth can remain in the air. Separate helium observations follow gas escaping much farther from the planet.

planets.name: GJ 1214 b
planets.hook: A world hidden by aerosols
planets.intro: GJ 1214 b is wrapped in thick clouds and haze that reflect much of its star’s light. They conceal a deep atmosphere and whatever lies beneath it. A water-rich interior is one possibility, with water buried under pressures far beyond those in Earth’s oceans.
planets.question: Why can a spectrum look almost flat?
planets.answer: High clouds and haze can block our view of deeper gas. They reduce the differences between wavelengths, leaving a much flatter transmission spectrum.
planets.evidence: For years, GJ 1214 b produced frustratingly flat transmission spectra. Thick aerosols can obscure the gas below and wash out its chemical fingerprints. Webb then watched the planet through an orbit in infrared light. Its changing brightness constrained how it moves heat and reflects starlight, while its deeper atmosphere remains hidden.

planets.name: LHS 3844 b
planets.hook: A dark rocky surface
planets.intro: A year on LHS 3844 b lasts about 11 hours. This small rocky world appears to have little atmosphere, leaving its surface exposed to its nearby star. Dark rock such as basalt could cover the ground, either in solid slabs or broken down into weathered dust.
planets.question: Can a telescope tell one rock from another?
planets.answer: Different minerals emit infrared light differently. Comparing the measured spectrum with laboratory rock spectra lets astronomers test possible surface materials. Several dark, low-silica materials fit this planet.
planets.evidence: Rock gives off infrared light with a pattern that depends on its minerals. Observations of LHS 3844 b can be compared with laboratory spectra of heated rocks. The Webb study finds a dark, largely featureless spectrum compatible with low-silica surface materials. Basalt is one candidate. The data allow both exposed slabs and weathered powder, so the texture of the ground remains an open question.

planets.name: TOI-561 b
planets.hook: A small hot planet that may have kept its atmosphere
planets.intro: TOI-561 b circles its star in less than 11 hours. A thick atmosphere may surround this intensely heated rocky world, above an ocean of molten rock. Gases dissolved in the molten interior could be released into the air, helping replenish what escapes to space.
planets.question: How could an atmosphere survive here?
planets.answer: Molten rock can store gases and exchange them with the atmosphere. Evolution models find some routes that preserve a thick atmosphere, although many starting conditions leave the planet bare.
planets.evidence: Webb measured the day-side infrared spectrum of TOI-561 b and found it cooler than the tested bare-rock cases. A thick atmosphere is a promising explanation. Models then ask how gas could survive so close to the star: a molten interior can store and release it over time. Carbon-dioxide-rich and sulfur-dioxide-rich envelopes are possible outcomes, rather than two measured compositions.

planets.name: Kepler-16 b
planets.hook: Two stars in the sky
planets.intro: Kepler-16 b travels around two stars in a 229-day year. The planet is similar to Saturn in mass and size. Its two suns move around each other while the planet follows a much wider path.
planets.question: Would the two suns always set together?
planets.answer: Their positions change as they orbit one another. From the planet, the two stars would move relative to each other in the sky. A specific sunset sequence also depends on the planet’s rotation and the observer’s location.
planets.evidence: Kepler saw this planet pass in front of both stars, alongside the eclipses the stars produce themselves. The changing timing and depth of those events let Doyle and colleagues untangle a three-body system. The planet circles the pair in about 229 days while the stars orbit each other much faster. From its atmosphere, the two suns would continually change their relative positions.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 b
planets.hook: The hot inner world of a compact family
planets.intro: TRAPPIST-1 b is the innermost of seven known planets around a tiny, cool star. Its hot day side and much colder night side suggest exposed rock with little atmosphere to carry heat between them.
planets.question: Why compare it with its neighbours?
planets.answer: The planets formed around the same star but receive different amounts of light. Comparing them helps test how small rocky worlds lose or retain their atmospheres.
planets.evidence: A substantial atmosphere can carry heat away from a planet’s day side. Webb’s infrared phase observations instead find a hot day side on TRAPPIST-1 b and no significant night-side emission. That pattern fits exposed rock with little air to move the heat. Comparing b with its neighbouring planets lets astronomers test how rocky worlds around the same star retain or lose atmospheres.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1 c
planets.hook: A rocky neighbour with a different heat signal
planets.intro: TRAPPIST-1 c is almost Earth-sized, with a year lasting just 2.4 days. Strong starlight heats this rocky world. Its surface may be bare, or covered by a thin atmosphere, with brighter rock reflecting more light than on its inner neighbour b.
planets.question: Is it another Venus?
planets.answer: It receives strong starlight, but its thermal observations disfavor a thick greenhouse atmosphere. A bare surface or a thinner, weak-greenhouse atmosphere remains possible.
planets.evidence: TRAPPIST-1 c is cooler in the measured infrared band than its inner neighbour b. Its faint night side still argues against a thick atmosphere that efficiently carries heat around the globe. A more reflective rocky surface is one explanation. A thin atmosphere with a weak greenhouse effect also remains possible. Those alternatives matter when asking why two nearby, similar-sized planets look different in heat.

planets.hook: A small planet in a temperate orbit
planets.intro: TRAPPIST-1 e is slightly smaller than Earth, with a year lasting about six days. It receives enough starlight for liquid water to be possible with a suitable atmosphere. Whether it has air or water remains open, so both bare rock and a milder world are still possibilities.
planets.question: Why is the star part of the problem?
planets.answer: Bright and dark regions on the star change the light we measure during a transit. That can imitate or obscure features from the planet’s atmosphere, so repeated observations are needed.
planets.evidence: TRAPPIST-1 e receives a level of starlight that makes liquid water possible with a suitable atmosphere. Finding that atmosphere is difficult. Webb measures the spectrum during transits, but bright and dark patches on the star can add their own signals. The published analyses test atmospheric models while accounting for this stellar interference. Air, oceans and habitability are still questions here.

planets.name: LHS 1140 b
planets.hook: A possible water-rich world
planets.intro: LHS 1140 b circles a cool star in about 25 days. Larger and heavier than Earth, it could hold a deep layer of water. One possible landscape is a frozen ocean with an open patch on the warmer day side. Far below, pressure could turn the water into dense ice above the rocky interior.
planets.question: Could an ocean have ice underneath it?
planets.answer: At great depth, pressure can turn water into dense forms of ice even when it is warm. A sufficiently water-rich planet could have these layers between an ocean and its rocky interior.
planets.evidence: Measuring a planet’s radius and mass lets astronomers ask which materials could fill it. LHS 1140 b is less dense than a simple Earth-like mixture would predict. A substantial water layer is one explanation explored in the interior models. With suitable air and temperature, its upper water could form an ocean or ice shell, while much higher pressure changes the water far below.

planets.hook: Methane above an unresolved interior
planets.intro: K2-18 b has a hydrogen-rich atmosphere containing methane. Beneath it, a deep ocean is one possibility. Another is a much hotter interior under a thick envelope of gas. We do not yet know whether this planet has a liquid surface at all.
planets.question: What happened to the claims about life?
planets.answer: Some analyses reported possible sulfur-bearing molecules. Independent reanalyses found that the evidence was not robust and that other molecules could explain the features. Methane has been detected more securely.
planets.evidence: Methane is a strong part of K2-18 b’s atmospheric spectrum. What lies below is much less settled: interior models can allow an ocean or a thick, much hotter fluid envelope. Reports of sulfur-bearing molecules attracted attention because of their possible biological associations. Independent analyses found that the claimed evidence was not robust. The spectra have not established life or an ocean on this planet.

planets.hook: A young giant we can separate from its star
planets.intro: HR 8799 e is a young gas giant still glowing with heat left over from its formation. It belongs to a family of four giant planets on wide orbits around the same star. Beneath its clouds lies a hot, dense interior that will cool over millions of years.
planets.question: What can four planets tell us that one cannot?
planets.answer: They share a star and formation environment. Differences in their atmospheric chemistry can help test how much gas and solid material each planet collected.
planets.evidence: HR 8799’s planets are young enough to shine in infrared light with heat left over from their formation. Blocking much of the star’s glare lets telescopes separate their light. Webb observations at wavelengths sensitive to carbon dioxide add to earlier atmospheric spectra. Comparing four planets around the same star helps researchers investigate how their gas and solid ingredients were collected.

planets.intro: 51 Eridani b is a young gas giant with methane and water vapour in its cloudy atmosphere. It still gives off heat from its formation, even far from its star. Deep below the clouds, increasing pressure turns the gas into dense fluid.
planets.question: Why do methane and carbon monoxide matter together?
planets.answer: Their relative amounts depend on temperature and how rapidly gas moves between layers. Seeing both helps test whether mixing carries gas upward faster than chemical reactions can adjust.
planets.evidence: The Gemini Planet Imager separated 51 Eridani b from the glare of its star and recorded strong methane absorption, alongside water. Its youth lets us see the planet through its own infrared glow. Observations across more wavelengths favour a partly cloudy atmosphere. The chemistry and brightness help test how young giants cool after forming.

planets.name: Beta Pictoris b
planets.hook: A giant with a roughly nine-hour spin
planets.intro: Beta Pictoris b is a young, hot giant that may spin once in roughly nine hours. It circles a star surrounded by a broad disc of dust, with another giant planet closer in. Heat left over from its formation keeps its atmosphere hot despite the distant star.
planets.question: How do you measure a planet’s spin?
planets.answer: One side of a rotating planet moves toward us while the other moves away. This broadens molecular lines in its spectrum. Converting the broadening into a period also requires a radius and an assumed viewing angle.
planets.evidence: A rotating globe sends light toward us from one side and away from us from the other. The resulting Doppler shifts broaden lines in its spectrum. High-resolution observations of Beta Pictoris b measure that broadening in molecular features. A spin period can then be estimated using a radius and a viewing angle. The estimated nine-hour day depends on the assumed radius and tilt.

planets.name: WASP-76 b
planets.hook: Iron in the air
planets.intro: WASP-76 b has iron vapour in its intensely heated atmosphere. As gas moves toward the cooler night side, some of that iron could condense into clouds or droplets. This giant circles its star in less than two days.
planets.question: Could it rain iron?
planets.answer: Iron can condense as an atmosphere cools. An uneven iron signal across the planet motivated the rain interpretation. Winds, temperature differences and clouds can also alter the signal, so the observations do not uniquely establish falling iron rain.
planets.evidence: Ehrenreich and colleagues measured an uneven iron-vapour signal as this planet crossed its star. One explanation is that iron carried from the hot day side condenses as it reaches cooler regions, possibly making iron rain. The spectrum detects the gas, rather than falling droplets. Temperature differences, winds and clouds also affect which parts of the atmosphere contribute to the signal.

planets.name: WASP-103 b
planets.hook: Stretched by its star
planets.intro: WASP-103 b orbits so close to its star that tides stretch its shape. Its silhouette is better described as a slightly elongated globe than a perfect sphere. A year passes in less than a day.
planets.question: Why would a planet stretch?
planets.answer: The star pulls more strongly on the near side than the far side. A fluid planet can deform under this difference. CHEOPS transit data favour a distorted shape at about three standard deviations.
planets.evidence: The star pulls more strongly on the planet’s near side than its far side. On this very close orbit, the difference can distort a fluid globe. Barros and colleagues tested that idea against the shape of CHEOPS transit light curves. Their data favour tidal deformation at about three standard deviations. Measuring the distortion more precisely could help constrain how material is distributed inside.

planets.name: KELT-9 b
planets.hook: A giant with metal vapour
planets.intro: KELT-9 b circles a star far hotter than the Sun. Its atmosphere is hot enough to contain iron and titanium as individual atoms and ions. Many molecules break apart on its blazing day side.
planets.question: How hot can a planet become?
planets.answer: Intense stellar radiation breaks molecular bonds and removes electrons from some atoms. Spectra of KELT-9 b contain neutral and ionised iron, and ionised titanium. These are atmospheric gases.
planets.evidence: KELT-9 b receives fierce radiation from a star hotter than the Sun. Hoeijmakers and colleagues searched high-resolution transit spectra for the signatures of metals and detected iron and ionised titanium. Such atoms can remain in the gas under these extreme conditions. Many molecules break apart at these temperatures.

planets.name: HD 80606 b
planets.hook: A year of extreme changes
planets.intro: HD 80606 b follows a long, stretched orbit. For most of its year it stays far from the star, then rushes close enough for a sharp burst of heating. Its atmosphere warms and cools as the stellar distance changes.
planets.evidence: HD 80606 b spends most of its long orbit far from its star, then rushes through a very close approach. Laughlin and colleagues followed that passage with Spitzer and measured a rapid rise in infrared brightness. It was a direct way to watch an atmosphere respond to a changing energy supply. The orbit’s stretched shape makes this natural heating experiment repeat each year.

planets.name: GJ 436 b
planets.hook: An atmosphere escaping into space
planets.intro: GJ 436 b is a warm Neptune-sized planet losing hydrogen into space. The escaping gas forms an enormous cloud extending far beyond the globe. Its orbit is slightly stretched, bringing it nearer to its star and farther away during each year.
planets.question: Would the escaping gas look like a comet?
planets.answer: The hydrogen cloud is detected in ultraviolet light. Its extended shape has been compared with a comet, but it would not appear as a bright visible tail to an unaided eye.
planets.evidence: Hubble detected a deep ultraviolet transit lasting far longer than the ordinary transit of GJ 436 b. Escaping hydrogen can explain this enormous absorbing cloud. Its shape has earned the planet comparisons with a comet. The observation follows ultraviolet absorption by gas, so the tail would not look like a bright comet tail in visible light.

planets.intro: GJ 9827 d is about twice as wide as Earth and has an atmosphere rich in water vapour. This is a hot world of steam, with a year lasting only about six days. Water in the air does not establish an ocean underneath.

planets.name: TOI-270 d
planets.hook: Methane and carbon dioxide above a deep interior
planets.intro: TOI-270 d has a hydrogen-rich atmosphere containing methane and carbon dioxide. About twice as wide as Earth, it could have a deep, hot mixture of water and gas below. Whether a separate liquid ocean exists remains unsettled.
planets.question: Can water and gas blend together?
planets.answer: At high pressure and temperature, an interior can contain a mixed fluid envelope. Other models allow a separate ocean. The measured gases alone do not settle which structure this planet has.
planets.evidence: Webb transmission spectra reveal methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of TOI-270 d. These molecules help constrain the mixture of gases and the conditions that supply them. The next question lies deeper: does the envelope meet a distinct ocean, or pass into a hot mixed fluid? Atmospheric chemistry narrows the possibilities, but a liquid-water boundary has not been found.

planets.hook: Close neighbours with different densities
planets.intro: A year on TOI-178 g lasts 20.7 days. It is about 2.9 times as wide as Earth. This system contains six planets packed onto short orbits. Five belong to a chain of linked orbital rhythms, while their densities vary sharply from one world to the next.
planets.question: Does orbital order mean matching interiors?
planets.answer: The outer five planets belong to a resonance chain. Their differing densities show that this orderly arrangement can contain planets with quite different amounts of gas and dense material.
planets.evidence: Observations with CHEOPS, ground-based telescopes and stellar-velocity measurements revealed six planets around TOI-178. The outer five follow a chain of linked orbital rhythms. planets.intro: Kepler-36 b is a dense rocky planet with a much larger neighbour on the next orbit out. The two planets pass remarkably close to one another, yet their interiors are very different. Planet b packs its material into a much smaller globe.
planets.question: How can neighbours be so different?
planets.answer: The mass and radius measurements favour a rocky planet b and a gas-rich planet c. A shared star does not guarantee matching planets. Their histories of gathering and losing gas can differ.

planets.name: Kepler-51 d
planets.hook: A remarkably light, swollen world
planets.intro: A year on Kepler-51 d lasts 130.2 days. It is about 0.87 times as wide as Jupiter. The three transiting planets in this young system spread very little mass across enormous globes. Their thick envelopes make them much less dense than the giant planets of our Solar System.
planets.question: How can a planet be so light for its size?
planets.answer: A low mean density means a large volume for a small mass. Gas envelopes and high-altitude aerosols can give these planets very large apparent radii. A fourth planet is inferred from changing transit times.
planets.evidence: Kepler-51’s transiting planets have unusually large radii for their small masses. When Webb observed d, its transit arrived far earlier than expected from a three-planet model. Combining that event with other transit times led to evidence for a fourth planet. The same gravitational timing method helps weigh the visible planets and establish how little material fills their enormous globes.

planets.answer: Orbital resonances mean that repeated gravitational nudges occur at related phases. Transit observations establish a chain linking the six known planets.

planets.intro: 51 Peg b is a hot giant with water vapour in its atmosphere. It circles a Sun-like star in just over four days. Because it does not transit the star, its physical size is harder to measure.

planets.name: Proxima Centauri b
planets.hook: A compact rocky world
planets.intro: Proxima Centauri b circles the nearest star to the Sun in about eleven days. Its minimum mass is close to Earth’s. We still do not know whether this small world has an atmosphere or a liquid-water surface.
planets.evidence: Proxima Centauri’s small, repeating velocity changes revealed a planet on an eleven-day orbit. That wobble gives a minimum mass because the orbit’s tilt is uncertain. The planet receives a level of starlight compatible with liquid water under suitable atmospheric conditions, but its atmosphere and radius have not been measured.
